question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I lean toward B (underestimate) here. For an all-or-nothing vaccine the incidence rate ratio implicitly assumes a constant hazard that doesn't really map to the underlying process once exposure heterogeneity is present; the mismatch with the usual leaky-vaccine framing then tends to pull the IRR below the true per-exposure efficacy. Not 100% sure without the exact derivation, but that seems the more likely direction of bias.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I lean toward C (correctly estimate) here, since the per-exposure definition of vaccine efficacy for an all-or-nothing vaccine seems to line up directly with how the incidence rate ratio is constructed—both focus on the reduction in infection probability per exposure event under the assumption of constant hazard. That said, I'm only about 30% confident because real-world heterogeneity in exposure rates could introduce some mismatch I haven't fully worked through.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is B, underestimate. For an all-or-nothing vaccine the protection is absolute once it takes, so any exposures after the first infection event become irrelevant to the outcome; the incidence rate ratio therefore undercounts the true per-exposure protective effect and produces an underestimate. I'm only moderately confident because the result might flip if exposure heterogeneity is extreme, but on the basic model it seems to point that way.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I'll hold off on committing to an answer in this initial round, as I'm still thinking through how exposure heterogeneity might interact with the all-or-nothing mechanism and whether the constant-hazard assumption even holds here.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Exposure heterogeneity across individuals likely means the 1-IRR will miss some of the all-or-nothing blocking effect and thus underestimate the true per-exposure VE (medium confidence, as constant-hazard assumptions rarely hold perfectly here).

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine (complete protection in a fraction p of recipients, zero protection in the rest), the average per-exposure efficacy equals p. The incidence rate ratio (IRR) is computed from observed cases per person-time in a cohort with ongoing exposure risk. Because unvaccinated susceptibles are depleted faster than the (smaller) susceptible pool in the vaccinated arm, the unvaccinated incidence rate falls relative to the vaccinated rate; consequently IRR moves toward 1 and 1-IRR falls below p. Thus the quantity underestimates per-exposure vaccine efficacy.

B. underestimate

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fraction \(p\) of recipients are fully protected (infection hazard 0) while the remainder have the same hazard \(\lambda\) as unvaccinated individuals. Under Poisson exposures the observed incidence rate among the vaccinated is therefore exactly \((1-p)\lambda\), so the incidence rate ratio equals \(1-p\) at every instant. Consequently \(1-\)IRR recovers \(p\), which is also the average per-exposure efficacy (the factor by which infection probability per contact is reduced). The estimator is therefore unbiased. 

C. correctly estimate

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The incidence rate (IR) is computed as cases divided by total person-time at risk. For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction \(p\) of recipients are completely protected (hazard 0) and the remainder \(1-p\) retain the full hazard \(\lambda\). Because the unprotected vaccinated subjects are depleted faster, the observed person-time contributed by the vaccinated arm is smaller than it would be under a constant hazard of \((1-p)\lambda\). Consequently the measured IR\(_v\) lies below \((1-p)\lambda\), the incidence-rate ratio falls below \(1-p\), and \(1-\)IRR therefore exceeds \(p\). This is precisely an overestimate of the all-or-nothing efficacy parameter (the quantity that would be interpreted as per-exposure protection if the vaccine were instead modeled as leaky). Hence the correct choice is A.

(The result is exact only in continuous time with exponential infection times; discrete-time or cumulative-incidence analyses produce analogous upward bias.)

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For all-or-nothing vaccines, a fraction ε of individuals are fully protected (risk reduced to 0 per exposure) and the remainder receive no protection. This produces a time-varying hazard: the observed incidence rate ratio (IRR) therefore begins at 1-ε but rises toward 1 as the unprotected vaccinated individuals are depleted. Consequently any average IRR exceeds 1-ε, which means that 1-IRR falls short of ε and underestimates the per-exposure vaccine efficacy. (By contrast, the cumulative-incidence ratio remains exactly 1-ε and recovers the correct value.)

B. underestimate

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fraction \(p\) of individuals are fully protected (per-exposure VE = 1) while the rest have zero protection. The average per-exposure VE is therefore exactly \(p\).

Incidence rates are computed from observed cases divided by observed person-time. Because fully protected individuals never become infected, the vaccinated arm contributes disproportionately more person-time while generating only \((1-p)\) of the eventual cases. Consequently the measured incidence-rate ratio falls below \(1-p\), so that \(1-\text{IRR}\) exceeds \(p\). The conventional 1-IRR estimator therefore overestimates per-exposure vaccine efficacy.

Answer: A. overestimate

(The result is the opposite of the leaky-vaccine case, where 1-IRR underestimates per-exposure protection; the distinction arises solely from differential depletion of the susceptible pool.)

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The key distinction here is between all-or-nothing vaccines (a fraction ε of individuals receive complete sterilizing immunity; the remainder receive none) versus leaky vaccines (every individual receives the same partial reduction in susceptibility).  

Under an all-or-nothing model the vaccinated group therefore contains a fixed fraction (1-ε) of fully susceptible individuals whose hazard is identical to that of the unvaccinated group. If λ(t) denotes the force of infection at calendar time t, the instantaneous incidence rate in the unvaccinated cohort is λ(t)·S(t) while that in the vaccinated cohort is (1-ε)λ(t)·S(t), where S(t) is the common survival function among susceptibles. Their ratio is therefore exactly 1-ε at every instant, so the incidence-rate ratio (and 1-IRR) recovers the per-exposure efficacy without bias.  

(The same algebra does not hold for leaky vaccines, whose IRR drifts over time because the entire vaccinated cohort experiences a uniformly lowered hazard.)  

Thus 1-IRR correctly estimates per-exposure vaccine efficacy for an all-or-nothing vaccine.  

Final answer: C. correctly estimate

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The correct answer is A (overestimate).

An all-or-nothing vaccine fully protects a fraction \(v = VE\) of recipients and has no effect on the remainder \(u = 1 - VE\). The quantity \(VE\) is also the average per-exposure efficacy, because a vaccinated person's infection probability per exposure is exactly \(u\) times that of an unvaccinated person.

Under a constant force of infection \(\lambda\), the observed incidence rate (cases per unit person-time) in the unvaccinated arm equals \(\lambda\). In the vaccinated arm the same events occur only among the unprotected fraction, but the protected individuals continue to contribute person-time without ever becoming cases. Consequently the denominator of the vaccinated incidence rate is inflated relative to the numerator, so
\[
IRR < u.
\]
Hence
\[
1 - IRR > VE.
\]
The incidence-rate-ratio estimator therefore overstates the true per-exposure efficacy. (The bias vanishes only in the limit of a vanishingly rare outcome, when protected person-time becomes negligible.)

Final answer: A. overestimate

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The all-or-nothing model assumes a fixed fraction \(f\) of vaccinated individuals receive complete (100%) protection while the remainder receive none. Under a constant hazard \(\lambda\) of infection per exposure, the instantaneous incidence rates are \(\lambda\exp(-\lambda t)\) (unvaccinated) and \(\lambda(1-f)\exp(-\lambda t)\) (vaccinated). Their ratio is therefore constantly \(1-f\), independent of time and depletion. Consequently \(1-\text{IRR}=f\), which equals both the proportion fully protected and the average per-exposure efficacy. Hence the quantity is estimated correctly (choice C).

(The same algebra shows that a leaky vaccine also yields an unbiased estimate, but that is outside the scope of the present question.)
